# ADR 0003 — Sweep population, and the below-floor descendant scope root

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-08-05
- **Amends:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D4
  ("Consult discipline: polled, not fallback") — extends the pointer consult to a
  descendant scope root reached through a stale `directChildScopeIndex` name
- **Restates:** [#26](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26) decision D2
  ("Cascade scope: root cut + background sweep") — the sweep's population is *interior
  nodes*, which the v2 blueprint's `### sweep` section lost; no change to the decision
  itself
- **Relates to:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D6
  (the direct-child-scope index and its self-heal)
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1025](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1025)

## Context

`SweepResolver` is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production
implementation. #1014 landed the other two and stopped short of this one, because the
sweep as built cannot obtain its own work-list.

The epoch-lag predicate in `sweep_pass` selects a node whose published record epoch is
below its scope's durable read-epoch floor. The adoption gate's stage 5 rejects exactly
those records (`floor::check`, `RejectionReason::EpochBelowFloor`). So a resolver built
the way `OwnerRotationNet::gated_root` is built refuses every node the sweep exists to
repair. The original framing of #1025 asked what should *authenticate* a below-floor
record so the owner can repair it. Two findings say that question has no good answer.

**Finding 1 — the sweep is walking the wrong population.** D2 of #26 splits the tree in
two: the **eager set** (the rotated scope root plus, as amended by #38 D5, every
transitively-reachable descendant scope root) is rotated *synchronously* by the cascade;
**interior nodes** "ride a background sweep re-sealing epoch-lagged nodes". `CONTEXT.md`
agrees — epoch lag is "a node whose envelope epoch is behind **its scope's** current
epoch; readable via history links". The implementation inverted this: `sweep_pass`
enumerates the eager set and applies the epoch-lag predicate to descendant scope roots,
the population the cascade already handles eagerly. The blueprint's `### sweep` section
is where the drift entered — it kept "the work-list is the epoch-lag predicate" from #26
D8 but dropped D2's statement of *what* lags.

**Finding 2 — a scope root cannot lag its own floor.** A scope root defines its scope's
epoch, and every floor advance is bounded by a record that already exists:

- `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both **publish first and raise the floor second**, so a
  crash between the two "never demands an unpublished epoch (no lockout)";
- `floor::advance_on_unseal` sets the floor *equal* to the adopted record's epoch;
- `cold_seed`'s `minReadEpoch` is owner-authored and, per #38 D3, bumps only on
  owner-triggered read rotations — which publish first.

So `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root never means "this node lags and needs
re-sealing". It means **the record we fetched is not the current one**. The most common
non-adversarial cause is a stale name: the parent's `directChildScopeIndex` still names
the child scope at a name a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved.

Two consequences of the drift are worth recording. The index self-heal (#38 D6: "a scope
root encountered but missing from its parent's index is repaired and flagged") is
implemented as canonicalisation performed *during* a lag re-seal, so it is unreachable
whenever the predicate is vacuous — and it is a different repair from the one D6
specifies. And `sweep_pass`'s only production caller is grant creation's convergence
gate (#26 D2: "Grant creation converges its subtree first"), whose `SubtreeNotConverged`
verdict therefore cannot fire: the gate passes vacuously, so "a new grantee cannot
regress through an ancestor scope's history" is currently unenforced.

## Decision

**D1 — the sweep's population is interior nodes.** Re-target the work-list at nodes
*within* a scope whose envelope epoch is behind the scope's current epoch, per #26 D2.
Descendant scope roots are eager-set members and are not swept. The blueprint's
`### sweep` section is corrected to say so.

**D2 — a below-floor scope root is a name-staleness signal, handled by a pointer
consult.** When a scope root's record is refused at gate stage 5, the resolver returns a
distinct *superseded* verdict — neither `Rejected` (a trust violation the caller must
not retry) nor `Unavailable` (a transport stall). The handler consults that scope's
pointer per #38 D4, re-resolves at the re-pointed `currentRootName`, and fails closed
only if the fresh record is still below the floor. This extends D4's consult discipline
from the cold-start/focus-tick root to any descendant scope root reached through a
possibly-stale index entry.

**D3 — the index self-heal is decoupled from any epoch comparison.** The D6 repair — a
scope root encountered during enumeration but missing from its parent's index — is
detectable from the walk alone. It runs on the enumeration result and is flagged there,
independent of whether any node is being re-sealed.

### Rejected alternatives

**A repair-role gate variant** that keeps stages 1–3 and 6 and substitutes an owner-held
committed set for the record's. Rejected on security, not just on need. The sweep reuses
the scope's **existing override seed verbatim** — it mints none. Admitting a below-floor
record would therefore republish the *old seed* at the current epoch, handing every
revoked reader who cached that seed a record that passes the gate. That is a full
revocation bypass, strictly worse than the stale-grant-set hole the variant was proposed
to close. The grant-set commitment is owner-signed and epoch-free by design, so it
carries no freshness of its own and cannot distinguish a replayed pre-rotation section;
the floor stages are the only thing that can.

**Re-sealing from owner-held state** rather than from the lagging record. Rejected on
architecture: the material a re-seal needs (each descendant's commitment, ledger, child
index, carried history links) would have to be mirrored locally, and #26 D8 fixes
"published records are the sole source of truth — no job records, no checkpoints".

## Consequences

- `SweepResolver` becomes implementable: its work-list is drawn from records the
  adoption gate *accepts*, so it composes with `OwnerRotationNet::gated_root` unchanged.
- The gate keeps its fail-closed posture at stage 5. Nothing is admitted below a floor;
  the below-floor case gains a *route* (consult and re-resolve), not an exemption. AGENTS
  rule 6 is preserved as written.
- Grant creation's convergence gate becomes able to fire. This is a behaviour change at a
  security-relevant gate that has been silently passing, and it needs its own coverage —
  tracked separately from the sweep re-targeting.
- A stale `directChildScopeIndex` entry stops being an unexplained hard rejection and
  becomes a self-correcting consult, which also narrows #38 D6's poisoning surface: a
  wrong name now costs a pointer round-trip instead of a fail-closed stall.
- The self-heal starts running, so `flaggedIndexes` becomes non-vacuous for the first
  time; hosts that surface it should expect real traffic.

## Gate

- A below-floor descendant scope root whose pointer re-points to a fresh record is
  converged after the consult; one whose fresh record is *still* below the floor is
  refused fail-closed. Distinct, asserted outcomes.
- A forged below-floor record is refused, and no consult path admits it.
- An interior node behind its scope's epoch is re-sealed to the current epoch;
  re-running the pass is a no-op (idempotence) and concurrent sweepers are safe under
  CAS.
- A scope root encountered but absent from its parent's index is repaired and flagged
  with no node re-sealed in the same pass — proving the self-heal no longer rides the
  epoch comparison.

# ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-08-05
- **Amends:** [#26](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26) decision D3
  ("Write plane: parallel flat write-seed tree; write rotation = override + child-first
  name wave") — makes concrete what "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors"
  requires, a clause the v2 blueprint dropped
- **Relates to:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D3
  (the re-point object supplies `currentRootName` only) and
  [#27](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) (the child-ref wire format)
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1026](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1026)

## Context

`rotateScopeWrite` mints a fresh write override seed and republishes the scope's whole
subtree under freshly derived names. Every per-node write artefact — `writeSeed`,
`writeKey`, and the Ed25519 IPNS keypair that *is* the `ipnsName` — derives from
`KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`, so a fresh scope seed moves every node in the subtree to
a new name.

D3 of #26 states how each class of party keeps up: "surviving write-grantees derive every
new name locally (zero re-discovery), read-only survivors follow **republished mirrors**
plus the mailbox re-point for the root". #38 D3 later replaced the mailbox with the
owner-signed scope pointer as canonical for the root. The "republished mirrors" half was
never elaborated, and in the v2 blueprint's `### rotateScopeWrite` section it is gone
entirely — the text now reads "read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point
object", which covers the root and nothing below it.

That leaves a real hole. A read-only grantee **cannot derive interior names**: the grant
blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants, so a read-only holder has no
`writeScopeSeed` and no way to compute `KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`. The re-point object
carries `currentRootName` and no other name. The only remaining route from the root to a
child is the parent's read-body child list — and `ChildRef` carries an `ipnsName` per
child (#27's wire format). After a name wave those entries name nodes that have moved;
once interior old names batch-retire, they name nothing.

So the wave as specified strands every read-only survivor one level below the root. This
is not an under-implementation of a charted mechanism: no mechanism was ever charted.
The engine's own module text asserts the opposite invariant — "The read plane is
untouched" — which is true of override seeds, read keys and `minReadEpoch`, but not of
read-body *bytes*.

## Decision

**The name wave rewrites read-body child names.** When the wave republishes a node, it
rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName` in that node's read body to the child's freshly derived
name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read
epoch. The existing child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known
before its parent publishes, so no second pass is needed.

Three consequences follow and are accepted as part of this decision:

1. **The republish is not byte-stable.** The read body changes, so the record cannot be
   reproduced verbatim from its predecessor. Any "carry the read body verbatim" language
   in the blueprint or in `rotateScopeWrite`'s contract is withdrawn.
2. **The publisher needs read-plane material** — the node's read key, and a nonce from
   the entropy seam for the re-seal. The write rotation therefore touches read-plane
   bytes while leaving read-plane *keys and epochs* untouched; the blueprint must say
   the narrower thing rather than "the read plane is untouched".
3. **The read epoch does not move.** A rewrite at the same epoch is not a read rotation
   and must not raise any read-epoch floor; `minReadEpoch` still carries unchanged, per
   #38 D1's rule that each plane's clock is authored by its own authority.

### Rejected alternatives

**Resolve children by node id through a write-plane index**, removing names from the read
body. Correct in the abstract — location-independent ids are what the write plane already
uses — but it is a `crates/core` wire-format change to #27's `ChildRef`, and it would
leave a read-only grantee needing a name lookup they still cannot perform. Rejected as
out of scope and insufficient on its own.

**Tombstone every migrated interior name** and let readers chase `movedTo`, instead of
rewriting anything. Rejected: #33's chase is depth-guarded, so a subtree deeper than the
guard breaks outright; and old names lapse at the 90-day EOL, so the approach defers the
break rather than removing it. It also multiplies the wave's publish count by keeping a
live tombstone per interior node, against #34 D4's retirement path.

## Consequences

- Read-only survivors traverse the subtree normally after a wave, which is what #26 D3
  intended and what its "republished mirrors" clause was pointing at.
- `rotateScopeWrite` is no longer describable as write-plane-only. The blueprint entry and
  the engine module header both need correcting; the honest statement is that the wave
  rewrites read-plane *metadata* while never re-keying it.
- Content bytes are still never re-encrypted (#26 D6). Only the child-name field of a
  folder's read body changes.
- The wave's cost per node rises by one read-body re-seal. It stays O(subtree) and stays
  background and parallel, so the shape of the cost is unchanged.
- A resumed wave is unaffected: `isRepublished` still answers from published state alone,
  and a node whose record already sits at the new name is skipped before any re-seal.

## Gate

- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName`
  resolves every node in the subtree — asserted at a depth greater than one, so a
  root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its
  children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave, while the
  write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name

Two ADRs recording design decisions taken while scoping the last two unimplemented
rotation seams in the v2 build.

## ADR 0003 — sweep population and below-floor scope roots

Implemented by FSM1/cipher-box#1025.

`SweepResolver` could not be built because the sweep's work-list is the set of records
its own adoption gate refuses. Two findings behind that:

- The sweep walks the **eager set** (descendant scope roots) and applies the epoch-lag
  predicate to it, but #26 D2 puts the eager set under the *cascade* and gives the sweep
  **interior nodes**. The blueprint's `### sweep` section kept the predicate from #26 D8
  and dropped D2's statement of what lags.
- A scope root cannot lag its own floor: `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both publish first
  and raise the floor second, `advance_on_unseal` sets the floor equal to the adopted
  epoch, and `minReadEpoch` only bumps on owner read rotations that publish first. So
  `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root always means the record fetched is not the
  current one — most often via a stale `directChildScopeIndex` name.

Decides: re-target the sweep at interior nodes; route a below-floor scope root through a
#38 D4 pointer consult rather than repairing it; decouple the #38 D6 index self-heal from
the epoch comparison. Rejects a repair-role gate variant on security grounds — the sweep
reuses the existing override seed verbatim, so admitting a below-floor record would
republish the old seed at the current epoch.

Also records a consequence worth its own tracking: grant creation's convergence gate
cannot currently fire, so the "a new grantee cannot regress through an ancestor scope's
history" property is unenforced today.

## ADR 0004 — read-body child names on the name wave

Implemented by FSM1/cipher-box#1026.

The name wave moves every node in a scope's subtree to a freshly derived name. Write
grantees derive the new names locally; a **read-only** grantee cannot, because the grant
blob carries `writeScopeSeed` only for write grants, and the re-point object supplies
`currentRootName` alone. Their only route below the root is the parent's read-body
`ChildRef.ipnsName`, which the wave leaves pointing at names it has just retired.

#26 D3 said read-only survivors "follow republished mirrors"; that clause was never
elaborated and is absent from the blueprint's `rotateScopeWrite` entry.

Decides: the wave rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName` and re-seals the read body under the
unchanged read key at the unchanged read epoch. Accepts that the republish is therefore
not byte-stable, that the publisher needs read-plane material, and that the read epoch
still must not move. Rejects both a `ChildRef` wire-format change and per-node `movedTo`
tombstones.

## Notes

- Both are **Proposed**; status flips to implemented when the cipher-box PRs merge, per

- Blueprint and `CONTEXT.md` amendments land in cipher-box alongside the code, not here —
  this repo's copies are the as-charted archive.
- Happy to split into one PR per ADR if you would rather review them separately.

input.content:
## Why this is not wiring

`SweepResolver` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`) is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production implementation. #1014 landed the other two — `ChildIndexResolver` and `ScopeRootPublisher` — as `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs::OwnerRotationNet`, and deliberately stopped short of this one because it was blocked on a design question rather than on plumbing.

That question is now answered by **ADR 0003 — Sweep population, and the below-floor descendant scope root** (`decisions/0003-sweep-population-and-below-floor-scope-roots.md`, FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting.** The answer is not the one the original scope assumed: the resolver could not obtain its work-list because the sweep is walking the wrong population, and the below-floor records it was meant to repair should not be repaired at all.

## What the ADR settles

**The sweep's population is interior nodes, not descendant scope roots.** #26 D2 puts the eager set — the rotated scope root plus every transitively-reachable descendant scope root — under the *cascade*, and gives the sweep the interior nodes that "ride a background sweep re-sealing epoch-lagged nodes". `CONTEXT.md` agrees: epoch lag is "a node whose envelope epoch is behind **its scope's** current epoch". The blueprint's `### sweep` section kept #26 D8's "the work-list is the epoch-lag predicate" and dropped D2's statement of *what* lags, and the implementation followed the blueprint.

**A scope root cannot lag its own floor.** `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both publish first and raise the floor second; `floor::advance_on_unseal` sets the floor equal to the adopted epoch; `minReadEpoch` bumps only on owner read rotations that publish first. So `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root always means the record fetched is not the current one — most often because the parent's `directChildScopeIndex` names it at a name a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved. The gate's stage-5 rejection is correct, and the repair is a pointer consult, not a re-seal.

**Consequently the current `sweep_pass` duplicates the cascade with a vacuous predicate.** It enumerates the eager set and calls `reseal_scope_root` — the cascade's job, landed over the real seams in #1053. Nothing it does can fire in production.

## Scope

1. **Re-target the sweep at interior nodes.** Enumerate the nodes *within* a scope from the scope root's read body, stopping at scope-root boundaries (those belong to the cascade), and select those whose envelope epoch is behind the scope's current epoch. Re-seal each under the current node seed at the current epoch via `net::author::author_child_envelope`, and CAS-publish. This replaces the `reseal_scope_root` path in `sweep_pass`, and `SweepTarget` collapses accordingly — an interior node carries no commitment, ledger, grant blobs, or ascent link, so most of the current struct is scope-root material that belongs to the cascade.
2. **Land the concrete resolver over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`,** reusing `OwnerRotationNet`'s gated read rather than growing a parallel one. With the population corrected it composes with `gated_root`/the child read path unchanged, because its work-list is drawn from records the adoption gate *accepts*.
3. **Route a below-floor scope root through a pointer consult.** Return a distinct *superseded* verdict — neither `Rejected` (a trust violation) nor `Unavailable` (a transport stall) — and have the handler consult that scope's pointer per #38 D4, re-resolve at the re-pointed `currentRootName`, and fail closed only if the fresh record is still below the floor.
4. **Decouple the index self-heal.** #38 D6's repair is "a scope root encountered but missing from its parent's index is repaired and flagged" — detectable from the enumeration walk alone. Run it on the walk result, independent of any epoch comparison. What is implemented today is canonicalisation performed *during* a lag re-seal, which is both a different repair and unreachable whenever the predicate is vacuous.
5. **Fix the grant-creation convergence gate.** `create_read_grant` (`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs`) is `sweep_pass`'s only production caller. Its `SubtreeNotConverged` verdict fires only on a lost CAS race, which only happens on a publish, which only happens for a lagging node — so with a vacuous predicate the gate passes unconditionally and "a new grantee cannot regress through an ancestor scope's history" (#26 D2, `CONTEXT.md` "Epoch-converged") is **unenforced today**. Re-targeting the sweep makes the gate able to fire; it needs its own coverage proving it does, including the negative case.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `blueprint/engine.md` `### sweep` corrected **in this PR** — the sweep's population is interior nodes, not the eager set
- [ ] `CONTEXT.md` "Epoch lag" and "Epoch-converged" reconciled with the above
- [ ] ADR 0003 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint and glossary are maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- An interior node behind its scope's epoch is re-sealed to the current epoch and published; a node already at the epoch is a no-op. Re-running the pass changes nothing (idempotence), and concurrent sweepers are safe under CAS.
- The walk stops at scope-root boundaries — a descendant scope root inside the subtree is **not** swept, asserted explicitly, so the cascade/sweep split cannot silently regress.
- A below-floor scope root whose pointer re-points to a fresh record converges after the consult; one whose fresh record is still below the floor is refused fail-closed. Distinct, asserted outcomes.
- A forged below-floor record is refused, and no consult path admits it.
- A scope root encountered but absent from its parent's index is repaired and flagged **with no node re-sealed in the same pass**, proving the self-heal no longer rides the epoch comparison.
- Grant creation over a subtree with a lagging interior node refuses with `SubtreeNotConverged`, and succeeds once that node converges — the gate proven live in both directions.

## Scoping note — needs a call before work starts

Item 1 is materially larger than "implement the concrete `SweepResolver`", which is what this issue's title still says. An interior-node lazy wave needs a new intra-scope walk and a child re-seal path (`author_child_envelope` exists; the enumeration and the rotation-side wrapper do not), and it invalidates most of the current `SweepTarget`. Items 2–5 are comparatively small once item 1 exists.

Options: keep it whole and retitle this issue, or split item 1 into a sibling issue that this one depends on. Worth deciding before anyone picks it up.

## Why this is not wiring

`WriteWavePublisher` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`) is the write-plane rotation's transport edge. #1014 landed the two read-plane seams over the real network plane and deliberately stopped short of this one: three of its five methods are plumbing, but `republish` cannot be implemented against the seam as it stands.

Both blocking questions are now answered by **ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave** (`decisions/0004-read-body-child-names-on-the-name-wave.md`, FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting** — it settles a second, larger gap that this issue originally did not name.

## What the ADR settles

**D1 — the publisher re-resolves; it is not handed the authoring material.** The record handed to `republish` carries only routing identity:

```rust
pub struct RepublishedNode {
    pub node_id: [u8; 16],
    pub new_name: IpnsName,
    pub write_epoch: u64,
    pub is_root: bool,
}
```

Authoring at `new_name` additionally needs the node's read body, the read key it seals under, and the predecessor name. Widening this struct does not work as stated, because the orchestrator does not hold that material either — `WriteScopeNode` is `{node_id, current_name, child_node_ids}` — so it would mean widening `WriteSubtreeResolver` too, and dragging O(subtree) bodies and per-node key material through a primitive that currently holds exactly one secret.

Instead: add **`current_name: IpnsName`** to `RepublishedNode`, and let the concrete publisher do the gated read at `current_name` and author at `new_name`. This mirrors the landed read-plane precedent — `OwnerRotationNet::publish_scope_root` already does exactly this, and says so in code: *"The read body and the envelope fields a republish preserves come from the node's own current record, gated — the rotation carries neither."* The resume contract stays trivially intact: `is_republished(new_name)` is unchanged and still answers from published state alone.

**D2 — the read body cannot be carried verbatim.** `ChildRef.ipns_name` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs`) lives in the **read** body. The wave moves every node in the subtree to a freshly derived name, so afterwards every parent's child refs name nodes that have moved, and once interior old names batch-retire they name nothing.

Write-grantees are fine — they derive names from `writeScopeSeed`. **Read-only survivors cannot**: `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant, and the re-point object carries `currentRootName` and no other name. So without a rewrite, a read-only grantee reaches the new root and cannot descend. #26 D3's "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors" was pointing at exactly this and was never elaborated; the blueprint dropped the clause entirely.

So the wave **rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName`** to the child's freshly derived name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read epoch. Child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known before its parent publishes.

## Scope

1. **Widen `RepublishedNode` with `current_name`** and update `rotate_scope_write`'s call site plus the simulation tests.
2. **Land the concrete `WriteWavePublisher`** over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`:
   - `register` / `retire` over `net::register` and `net::retire` — already bounded and idempotent, reuse rather than duplicate;
   - `is_republished` over the fan-out GET;
   - `republish` over the gated read at `current_name`, the read-body child-name rewrite, then `net::author` + `net::record_publish`, signing under `kdf::ipns_keypair(write_seed(freshWriteScopeSeed, node_id))`;
   - `publish_repoint` across the three channels — scope pointer, mailbox, old-root tombstone.
3. **Thread the read-plane material the rewrite needs** — the node's read key, and a nonce from the entropy seam. The read epoch must **not** move: a same-epoch rewrite is not a read rotation and must raise no read-epoch floor (#38 D1, each plane's clock authored by its own authority).
4. **Root linger stays**: `retire` must never include the old root name, and `root_retire_ready` is still stubbed `false` pending the migration-window constant.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `blueprint/engine.md` `### rotateScopeWrite` corrected **in this PR** — the wave rewrites read-plane metadata while never re-keying it; "read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point object" is incomplete on its own
- [ ] `blueprint/core.md` notes the read-body re-seal at an unchanged read epoch, since the sealing contract is its territory
- [ ] The engine module header's "The read plane is untouched" claim narrowed to keys and epochs
- [ ] Any "carry the read body verbatim" / byte-stable-republish language withdrawn — the body changes, so the record is not byte-stable
- [ ] ADR 0004 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint is maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- Resumed name waves via the write-plane history link, and crash recovery from published records only, per #635.
- Register-first ordering enforced **structurally**, so a publish of an unregistered name is impossible rather than merely unlikely.
- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName` resolves **every** node in the subtree — asserted at depth greater than one, so a root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave while the write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name behind.

Folds the two merged ADRs into the normative corpus. Documentation only — no code surface, so the mandatory review gates are exempt per AGENTS.md.

Traceability: every mention links to the ADR file in cipher-box-next.

## `blueprint/engine.md` — `### sweep`

The section named the epoch-lag predicate (#26 D8) but never said *what* lags. #26 D2 puts the eager set under the **cascade** and gives the sweep **interior nodes**; the blueprint dropped that half, and the implementation followed the blueprint — so `sweep_pass` walks descendant scope roots and calls `reseal_scope_root`, duplicating the cascade under a predicate that cannot fire there.

Restates the interior-node population, and adds the below-floor rule: rotations publish *before* raising the floor, so a scope root below its own read-epoch floor cannot mean the root lags — it means the record fetched is stale, typically a `directChildScopeIndex` entry naming a root a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved. That routes to the #38 D4 pointer consult, never a repair, because the sweep reuses the scope's existing override seed verbatim and republishing it at the current epoch would be a revocation bypass.

Also records that the #38 D6 index self-heal is a walk-time repair independent of any re-seal.

## `blueprint/engine.md` — `### rotateScopeWrite`

"Read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point object" is true and insufficient: the re-point carries `currentRootName` and nothing below it. A read-only grantee holds no `writeScopeSeed` (the grant blob carries it only for write grants) and so can derive no interior name — their only route down is the parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName`, which the wave has just invalidated.

Adds the rewrite, and the three things it costs: the republish is not byte-stable, the wave touches read-plane *metadata* while never re-keying it, and the read-epoch floor never moves.

## `blueprint/core.md` — child refs

"Child writes never republish the parent" needed a carve-out: the name wave moves every child's `ipnsName` at once, so it does rewrite the parent's refs. Notes that this is a metadata rewrite at the unchanged read epoch, and that a node's *own* body still moves names untouched because `ipnsName` is not in the AAD (#39 D7) — the decision that makes the wave possible in the first place.

## `CONTEXT.md`

"Lazy wave" said "a scope's descendants", which reads as descendant scope roots. Tightened to interior nodes. "Epoch lag", "Eager set" and "Epoch-converged" were already correct and are untouched.

## Note on the diff

`blueprint/core.md`'s crypto-suite table shows a whitespace-only reformat. That table was already non-conformant on `main`; lint-staged runs `prettier --write` over any staged `.md`, so it normalizes on the first commit that touches the file. Unrelated to the content change.

## Follow-on

The code changes these decisions imply are tracked in #1025 and #1026, whose bodies now carry the ADR links and a checklist item to flip each ADR's `Status:` to implemented once the code PR merges.
EOF

`blueprint/*.md` + `CONTEXT.md` edits land in their **own docs-only PR** in cipher-box —

All three done, and #1058/#1061 merged while I was working.

## Blueprint → [#1066](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1066) (draft)

Docs-only, so exempt from the review gates. Every ADR mention links to the file in cipher-box-next — five links, all verified to resolve.

- **`engine.md` `### sweep`** — restates #26 D2's interior-node population, plus the below-floor rule and why admitting such a record would be a revocation bypass rather than a repair.
- **`engine.md` `### rotateScopeWrite`** — the child-ref rewrite, and its three costs.
- **`core.md` child refs** — the carve-out to "child writes never republish the parent". Checking this section turned up the decision that makes the whole wave possible: **#39 D7 deliberately keeps `ipnsName` out of the AAD** *"the name wave republishes epoch-lagged bodies under fresh names"*. So a node's own body moves names untouched — the original "carry the read body verbatim" instinct was right for the node itself, and only wrong for the **parent's** refs. That's now stated explicitly, which is the sharpest form of the finding.
- **`CONTEXT.md`** — "Lazy wave" said "a scope's descendants"; tightened to interior nodes. **"Epoch lag", "Eager set" and "Epoch-converged" were already correct** and I left them alone — narrower than the DoD I'd written earlier.

One diff artifact called out in the PR body: `core.md`'s crypto-suite table shows a whitespace-only reformat. It was already non-conformant on `main`, and lint-staged runs `prettier --write` on any staged `.md`.

## Issue bodies rewritten

Both now lead with the ADR link and what it settles, with restructured Scope and Gate sections. The blueprint items are checked off against #1066; what remains is code plus the ADR status flip.

**#1025** folds in the convergence gap as scope item 5, stated plainly: `SubtreeNotConverged` fires only on a lost CAS race, which needs a publish, which needs a lagging node — so with a vacuous predicate the gate passes unconditionally and *"a new grantee cannot regress through an ancestor scope's history"* is unenforced today. Its gate requires proving the check fires in both directions.

**One thing I flagged rather than decided,** at the end of #1025: re-targeting the sweep at interior nodes needs a new intra-scope walk and a child re-seal path, and invalidates most of `SweepTarget`. `author_child_envelope` exists, but the enumeration and rotation-side wrapper don't. That's materially bigger than the issue's title still claims, and items 2–5 are small once it exists. Keep it whole and retitle, or split item 1 into a sibling this depends on — worth deciding before anyone picks it up.

## State

`main` has #1058 and #1061 (merged 08:11–08:12Z). **#1066 is the only open PR** — 7 pass, 1 pending, 16 skipping.

Since #1058 and #1061 landed, the four-way verification is moot — they're all in `main` now. Worth a single verification run against current `main` instead; say the word and I'll kick it off.

`macroscope` was added as a PR review tool on FSM1/cipher-box on **2026-08-05**, joining
CodeRabbit and Greptile (Greptile quota resets mid-Aug 2026). Three reviewers now.

**It reviews DRAFT PRs.** This is the big behavioural difference: on #1066 CodeRabbit
posted *"Review skipped — Draft detected"* while macroscope submitted a real review with
inline findings at 08:13:50Z, ~1 min after the PR opened. So the keep-PRs-draft
convention (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing]]) no longer means "no
review" — it means "no CodeRabbit review".

**Where its output lands.** Author login is **`macroscopeapp[bot]`**. The review event
itself (`pulls/N/reviews`) is `COMMENTED` with an **empty body** — the findings are
inline `pulls/N/comments` entries. So a poller that reads only review *bodies* sees
nothing, the mirror of the CodeRabbit trap in
[[project-coderabbit-verdict-two-surfaces]]. Poll `pulls/N/comments` and filter on
`.user.login`.

**Finding format:** severity emoji + level (`🟠 **High**`), a `file:line` anchor, prose,
then a collapsible *"Reply 'fix it for me' or copy this AI Prompt"* block. Do **not** reply
"fix it for me" — same rule as every other reviewer: a finding is a symptom report, not a
spec (see [[feedback-never-apply-review-suggestions-literally]]).

**Signal quality, first data point: good.** On #1066 it caught a genuine cross-section
contradiction in a docs-only diff — the `sweep` section was re-scoped to interior nodes
while an *unedited* section 170 lines away still listed the sweep among
`reseal_scope_root`'s callers. It reasons across the whole file, not just the diff hunk,
which is exactly the class CodeRabbit's diff-scoped review misses.

**How to apply:** on any PR, check `pulls/N/comments` for `macroscopeapp[bot]` even while
the PR is a draft and even when CodeRabbit reports "Review skipped". When a finding names
an unchanged section, verify the contradiction against the file before editing — and
prefer correcting the stale section over relaxing the new one.

It flagged that `### sweep` now scopes the operation to interior nodes while the **owner write-seed cold-start** section 170 lines away still listed the sweep among `reseal_scope_root`'s callers:

`SweepResolver` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`) is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production implementation. #1014 landed the other two — `ChildIndexResolver` and `ScopeRootPublisher` — as `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs::OwnerRotationNet`, and deliberately stopped short of this one because it was blocked on a design question rather than on plumbing.

That question is now answered by **[ADR 0003 — Sweep population, and the below-floor descendant scope root](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0003-sweep-population-and-below-floor-scope-roots.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting.** The answer is not the one the original scope assumed: the resolver could not obtain its work-list because the sweep is walking the wrong population, and the below-floor records it was meant to repair should not be repaired at all.

## What the ADR settles

**The sweep's population is interior nodes, not descendant scope roots.** #26 D2 puts the eager set — the rotated scope root plus every transitively-reachable descendant scope root — under the *cascade*, and gives the sweep the interior nodes that "ride a background sweep re-sealing epoch-lagged nodes". `CONTEXT.md` agrees: epoch lag is "a node whose envelope epoch is behind **its scope's** current epoch". The blueprint's `### sweep` section kept #26 D8's "the work-list is the epoch-lag predicate" and dropped D2's statement of *what* lags, and the implementation followed the blueprint.

**A scope root cannot lag its own floor.** `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both publish first and raise the floor second; `floor::advance_on_unseal` sets the floor equal to the adopted epoch; `minReadEpoch` bumps only on owner read rotations that publish first. So `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root always means the record fetched is not the current one — most often because the parent's `directChildScopeIndex` names it at a name a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved. The gate's stage-5 rejection is correct, and the repair is a pointer consult, not a re-seal.

# Resolve PR Review Comments

Resolve all open review comments on the current PR from any automated reviewer (CodeRabbit, GitHub Copilot, etc.) or human reviewers.

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PR

```bash
PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr view --json number --jq '.number')
```

If no PR exists for the current branch, stop and inform the user.

### 2. Fetch all unresolved review threads

Use the GraphQL `reviewThreads` query to get threads with `isResolved` status:

```bash
REPO_OWNER=$(gh repo view --json owner --jq '.owner.login')
REPO_NAME=$(gh repo view --json name --jq '.name')

gh api graphql -f query="
{
  repository(owner: \"$REPO_OWNER\", name: \"$REPO_NAME\") {
    pullRequest(number: $PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first: 100) {
        nodes {
          id
          isResolved
          comments(first: 10) {
            nodes {
              id
              author { login }
              body
              path
              line
              createdAt
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}"
```

Filter to only unresolved threads. If none, report "No unresolved review threads" and stop.

### 3. Triage each comment

For each unresolved thread, read the comment and the referenced code. Categorize as:

- **Valid fix needed** — the comment identifies a real bug, security issue, or meaningful improvement
- **Already addressed** — the issue was fixed in a later commit on this branch
- **Not applicable** — the suggestion doesn't apply (explain why)

### 4. Implement fixes

For all "valid fix needed" comments:

1. Read the referenced file and understand the context
2. Implement the fix
3. Track which thread the fix addresses

Do NOT:

- Make unrelated changes or refactors
- Add features beyond what the comment requests
- Increase timeouts or add retries as a first approach — fix root causes

### 5. Run tests locally

After ALL fixes are implemented:

```bash
# Type check
pnpm typecheck

# Run relevant unit tests
pnpm test

# If E2E-relevant changes were made, run E2E tests too
cd tests/web-e2e && pnpm exec playwright test
```

Do NOT proceed to commit until tests pass. If tests fail, fix the failures first.

### 6. Commit and push

```bash
git add <specific-files>
git commit -m "fix: address PR review comments"
git push
```

### 7. Reply to and resolve each thread

For each thread, reply explaining what was done, then resolve:

- **Fixed comments**: Reply with what was changed and where, then resolve
- **Already addressed**: Reply explaining which commit addressed it, then resolve
- **Not applicable**: Reply with clear reasoning for not making changes, then resolve

Reply via REST (use `--field` not `-f` for `in_reply_to` — must be integer):

```bash
gh api repos/$REPO_OWNER/$REPO_NAME/pulls/$PR_NUMBER/comments \
  --field in_reply_to=COMMENT_ID \
  --raw-field body='...'
```

Resolve via GraphQL (can batch multiple):

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation {
  resolveReviewThread(input: {threadId: "THREAD_ID"}) {
    thread { isResolved }
  }
}'
```

### 8. Report summary

Print a summary table:

- Thread count resolved
- Fixes made (with file:line references)
- Comments marked as already addressed or not applicable

content.text:
All threads resolved on **#1066**. All four findings were real, and one was my own regression.

| # | File | Finding | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `core.md:120` | Read key not stated as unchanged | Fixed |
| 2 | `engine.md:427` | Index repair vs below-floor ordering | Fixed, reworded |
| 3 | `engine.md:447` | "override seeds" unqualified | Fixed |
| 4 | `engine.md:584` | "Every reseal" contradicts sweep exception | Fixed |

Commit `eb85d3185`.

**#3 and #4 were the ones worth having.** In the `rotateScopeWrite` section I wrote *"override seeds, read keys and `minReadEpoch` still carry verbatim"* twelve lines below *"fresh write override seed"* — unqualified, that reads as preserving the **write** seed, and the wrong reading is precisely the one that would let a revoked writer keep publishing. Now scoped to the read override seed.

**#4 was residue from my own `ce9892d81`** — the macroscope fix. That commit added the sweep exception to the end of the paragraph and struck the sweep from the parenthetical, but left the opening *"Every reseal authors an owner-write-blob"* absolute. So the paragraph asserted a universal and contradicted it two sentences later. Scoping the opening to write-body-publishing reseals makes the sweep exception *follow* from the rule rather than sit against it. Fixing one reviewer's finding introduced the next one's — worth noting.

For **#2** I didn't take the proposed wording. The self-heal (a missing entry in a parent index) and the below-floor rule (don't re-seal that root) act on *different objects*, so ordering them alone wouldn't have closed anything. The actual hazard is narrower: repairing an index entry with the **superseded** name — the one that caused the below-floor classification — would re-poison the entry the walk was healing. So the invariant is about which name may be written, not sequencing.

Issue numbers referenced from Rust source in `crates/`, checked against the tracker:

## Why the pattern fails

A comment naming a ticket makes a claim about the **tracker**, not the code. The tracker changes independently, so nothing in CI, review, or the type system can catch the claim drifting. It rots silently and asymmetrically: the comment stays put while the issue closes, splits, gets re-scoped, or turns out to have named the wrong thing.

Four went stale in `crates/engine/src/rotation/` alone within a week: `#745`/`#746` closed (leaving 25 refs pointing at nothing), `#1014` closed on merge, `#1025` named the wrong seam entirely, and `sweep.rs` still claimed tests fake `ScopeRootPublisher` after its production impl landed.

This also fights the existing `AGENTS.md` comment rules, which already warn that prose about paths *not* in the code "rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired".

## The rule

State the **condition**, not the ticket:

- `the real wiring is #1026` becomes `the real wiring is not landed`
- `deferred to #1025` becomes `no production implementation yet; tests fake this`

The condition is verifiable from the code and stops being true exactly when someone writes the impl — in the same diff that falsifies the comment. Dependencies run one way: issues point at code, code does not point back. An issue naming a stale path is a nuisance; code naming a stale issue is a lie a reader cannot cheaply check.

**Keep** the substantive prose these refs are usually attached to — binding contracts, fail-closed obligations, wire-format invariants, blueprint citations. That is the part worth having and it does not rot. This is a scalpel on the `#NNNN` tokens, not a comment purge.

## Scope

1. Sweep `crates/`, `apps/` and `packages/` for `#NNNN` in comments; replace each with the condition it stood for, or delete it where the surrounding sentence carries no information without it.
2. Keep blueprint/`CONTEXT.md` cross-references — those name durable documents, not tickets.
3. Add a CI guard so this does not regrow: fail on a `#\d{3,4}` token in a comment outside an allowlist. Without the guard the cleanup is a one-off that decays immediately.
4. Land as its own PR, separate from feature work — it touches many files and would otherwise drown a review diff.

#1030 converted the **seam-wiring** refs in `crates/engine/src/rotation/` as the worked example of the target shape. That module still carries 18 other refs — `#744`, `#746`, `#747`, `#756` (all closed, 11 refs) and `#752`, `#754`, `#764`, `#778` (open, 7 refs) — so it is a shape reference, not a finished directory.

Note the `#746` refs are decoration on a durable label: the sentences read "the label-conflict abort (C2, #746)". `C2` is the name worth keeping; the ticket adds nothing.

## Out of scope

Commit messages and PR bodies, which are timestamped artifacts where a ticket reference is correct and does not rot.

# Brief: strip tracker-issue references from code comments (cipher-box #1031)

Repo: `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box`, branch `chore/drop-tracker-refs-from-comments`.

## The rule

A comment that names a GitHub issue (`#1234`) makes a claim about the **tracker**,
not the code. The tracker moves independently, so nothing in CI, review, or the type
system catches the claim drifting. 86% of the refs in `crates/` already point at
closed issues.

**State the condition, not the ticket.** The condition is verifiable from the code
and stops being true in the same diff that falsifies the comment.

- `the real wiring is #1026` → `the real wiring is not landed`
- `deferred to #1025` → `no production implementation yet; tests fake this`
- `the label-conflict abort (C2, #746)` → `the label-conflict abort (C2)`
  (`C2` is the durable name; the ticket adds nothing — just delete the ref)
- `Regression test for #924.` → say what the regression **is**:
  `A crash between releasing a staged leaf and marking it must not destroy a
  successful upload.`

## Hard constraints

1. **This is a scalpel on the `#NNNN` tokens, not a comment purge.** Keep every bit
   of substantive prose these refs hang off — binding contracts, fail-closed
   obligations, wire-format invariants, blueprint citations. That prose is the part
   worth having and it does not rot.
2. **Never delete a whole comment** unless the sentence carries no information at
   all once the ref is gone (e.g. a bare `// see #820` on its own line, or a test
   named `// #924` with nothing else). When in doubt, keep and rewrite.
3. **Do not change code, tests, identifiers, or behaviour.** Comments and prose
   strings only. The one exception: `assert!`/`expect` **message** strings that
   name an issue — treat those exactly like comments (drop the ref, keep the
   sentence). Do not change the assertion itself.
4. **Do not run any `git`, `cargo`, `pnpm`, or `npx` command.** Do not commit, do
   not format, do not build. Other agents are editing other files in this same
   checkout concurrently. Edit **only** the files in your assigned list.
5. Keep references to durable documents — `blueprint/engine.md`, `CONTEXT.md`,
   `AGENTS.md`, RFC numbers, spec section names. Those name documents, not tickets.
6. Do not introduce **absence-justifying** prose — do not add sentences explaining
   why some path that is *not* in the code does not happen. State what the present
   code does.
7. Comments stay short. If the ref was load-bearing and the replacement condition
   needs more than a clause, you are probably over-explaining — prefer the shortest
   true statement.
8. Rewrap the affected comment paragraph to the width the surrounding comments use
   (Rust doc comments in this repo wrap at ~80 columns). Do not touch lines your
   edit did not make ragged.

## Deciding the replacement

Most refs fall into three shapes:

- **Decoration on a durable name** — `(C2, #746)`, `(the floor law, #685)`.
  Just delete the ref and its separator. No rewording.
- **A deferral / not-yet-wired claim** — `deferred to #1026`, `real wiring is #1025`.
  Replace with the condition: `not landed`, `no production implementation yet;
  tests fake this`. **Verify against the code first** — several of these have since
  been implemented, in which case say what is actually true now (or drop the clause).
- **A provenance note on a test** — `Regression test for #924`,
  `covers #820`. Replace with the invariant the test pins, in one clause.

An issue-state map is at `SCRATCH/issue-map.tsv` (`#N<TAB>STATE<TAB>title`). The
title usually tells you what the ref stood for without opening anything. Use
`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh issue view N --repo FSM1/cipher-box --json body --jq .body`
only when the title is not enough — and sparingly.

Beware: a **closed** issue does not mean the surrounding claim is now false. A
comment saying "tests fake this, real wiring is #1029" where #1029 is closed means
the wiring probably **landed** — check the code before writing "not landed".

## False positives — leave these alone

- CSS hex colours: `'#006644'`
- HTML entities: `▼`

## Report back

- The number of refs you removed, per file.
- Any ref you deliberately **kept**, and why.
- Any case where the code contradicted the comment (e.g. the comment said "not
  wired" but the production impl exists) — name the file and what you found. These
  are the interesting ones; call them out separately.

Closes #1031.

## What

Removes **442 tracking-issue references** across **123 distinct issues** and **127 files**, replacing each with the condition it stood for, and adds a CI guard so the pattern cannot regrow.

**112 of the 123 issues were already closed — 91%.**

The diff is line-neutral by construction (590 insertions, 590 deletions before the guard and docs): this is a scalpel on the `#NNNN` tokens, not a comment purge. Every binding contract, fail-closed obligation, wire-format invariant and blueprint citation the refs were hanging off is preserved.

## Why the pattern fails

A comment naming a ticket makes a claim about the **tracker**, not the code. The tracker changes independently, so nothing in CI, review, or the type system can catch the claim drifting. It rots silently and asymmetrically — the comment stays put while the issue closes, splits, or gets re-scoped.

Dependencies run one way: issues point at code, code does not point back. An issue naming a stale path is a nuisance; code naming a stale issue is a lie a reader cannot cheaply check.

## The three shapes, and what each became

| Shape | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decoration on a durable name | `the label-conflict abort (C2, #746)` | `the label-conflict abort (C2)` |
| A deferral claim | `the real wiring is #1026` | `the real wiring is not landed` |
| Test provenance | `Regression test for #924.` | the invariant the test actually pins |

## Four stale claims the sweep surfaced

Each of these was a comment asserting something the code had already contradicted — the failure mode the issue predicts, found in the wild:

- **`packages/client/src/transport.ts`** claimed the broadcast transport "is the next slice (#640)". It had landed: `broadcastTransport.ts` exists and `index.ts` already exports `BroadcastTransport`, `LeaderElection` and `LeaderRelay`. Rewritten to the present tense.
- **`crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs`** header excluded "content bytes (#868)" from the slice. The module owns a full content plane today — `publish_update_content`, `upload_version`, `upload_block`, quota classification. Only the cross-scope re-seal exclusion is still true, and only that remains.
- **`crates/engine/src/sync/op.rs`** attributed a quote to the wrong document: `(CONTEXT.md #632 scope: "does NOT land: scope-exit rotation triggering")`. That string is not in `CONTEXT.md` — it is issue #632's scope statement. The preceding clause already says the slice queues the trigger without rotating, so the parenthetical went.
- **`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs`** said "the production resolver/publisher this composes over lives in `crate::net::rotation`". Only the publisher half is true — `SweepResolver` still has no production impl and is faked everywhere. Now says so.

Two more of the same class, caught while sweeping and fixed here since they rot identically without being `#NNNN` tokens:

- `crates/contract/tests/contract.rs` — "This is the write path's first live coverage", a provenance claim that ages the moment a second suite lands.
- `apps/web/src/components/layout/NavItem.tsx` — `title="coming soon - #643"` shipped a tracker number to end users in a tooltip. No test asserts on the string (web-e2e targets `data-testid="nav-item-*"`).

## The guard

`scripts/check-tracker-refs.mjs`, run as `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` and wired into CI as a merge-blocking **Tracker Refs** job. It scans tracked `.rs`/`.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`-family files under `crates/`, `apps/`, `packages/`, `landing/` and `tools/`.

Two deliberate choices:

- **Scope is wider than the issue asked for.** `#1031` names `crates/`, `apps/` and `packages/`; leaving a first-party directory unguarded is how the pattern regrows, and `tools/hw-gates` already had two refs — one of which printed `issue #644` to a tool's **stdout**. Both fixed here.
- **Repo-qualified references are exempt, and fall out for free.** `FSM1/cipher-box-next#32` names a durable decision record in the wayfinder corpus; a bare `#644` names a ticket. The `\w` lookbehind that excludes HTML entities also excludes anything preceded by a repo name, so the blueprint's citation style keeps working and only bare tracker numbers fail.

CSS hex colours (`#006644`), HTML entities (`▼`) and Rust format specs (`{:#010o}`) are excluded structurally rather than by allowlist.

## Deliberately kept

Two-digit `#NN Dn` citations (`#33 D6`, `#26 D2`, `#39 D4`) name decisions in the frozen `FSM1/cipher-box-next` wayfinder corpus, not tickets — the same durable-name case as `C2`. They are below the guard's `{3,4}` threshold and were left alone. One sweep agent stripped two of them; both were restored.

## The rule now has a home

Added to `AGENTS.md` as a third bullet beside the two comment smells it belongs with — the issue notes this pattern already fought the existing rule against prose that "rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired". The gate is registered in `blueprint/testing.md`'s PR-gate tier per testing law 1.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `cargo fmt --all --check` | pass |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace` | 1404 passed |
| wasm32 check (`engine` + `wasm`) | clean |
| `pnpm typecheck` | pass |
| `pnpm test` | 656 passed (client 368 / api 178 / web 110) |
| `pnpm lint` | pass |
| `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` | 0 refs in 506 source files |

Review gates: `/simplify`, `/security-review` and `/crypto-privacy-review` were run as manual passes against their checklists — the slash-command skills are not installed in this environment.

content.text:
Both reviews came back with real findings. Here's where things stand.

**The security review's highest finding is one I can't fix inside this PR.** `Tracker Refs` is not in `main`'s branch-protection required contexts — I confirmed the live list has 19 entries and it isn't among them. Meanwhile this PR files the gate under "**PR gate** — merge-blocking" in `blueprint/testing.md` and says "Enforced by" in `AGENTS.md`. As shipped, both docs overstate it: a red `Tracker Refs` would merge.

That's a repo settings change, outside the diff, and it has to happen **after** this merges — adding a context that doesn't yet exist on `main` would leave every open PR hanging on a check that never reports. Your call, and I'd want your say-so before touching branch protection either way.

**The widened guard immediately paid for itself.** The security pass found the extension and root lists were too narrow — and the proof was four live refs in `ci.yml` itself, the very file this PR edits, plus three more in `.toml`/`.json` comments. Seven refs the original guard was structurally blind to. Now scanning 611 files instead of 506, all clean.

Three more script defects, all confirmed by running them:

- **Vacuous pass.** `git ls-files` exits 0 on a pathspec matching nothing, so a renamed root would silently drop out and the gate would pass having scanned zero files. Reproduced exactly that. Now asserts every root contributed files.
- **`{3,4}` breaks silently at 5 digits.** The repo is at #1067. Widened to `{3,5}` — and the upper bound is load-bearing, not a guess: it's what rejects 6- and 8-digit hex colours. Said so in the comment, because the obvious "simplification" to `{3,}` would flag every `#006644`.
- **`PR#820` slipped through** the lookbehind that exempts `owner/repo#32`. Replaced with an explicit qualified-prefix test, and added this repo's own issue URLs, which rot identically.

**The simplify pass caught me breaking my own new rule.** The comment I put on the CI step — "The scan reads the git index and the working tree only — no install" — explains why a `pnpm install` that *isn't there* isn't there. That's the absence-justifying shape, and I added the bullet banning it in the same diff. Deleted, along with the now-unnecessary pnpm setup.

It also caught two prose defects worth naming. `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` now claimed the `OpId` "the write plane claims" — verified: nothing claims it, that string appears nowhere else in `crates/`, and the helper discards it. And `rotate_write.rs` turned "reclaim is tracked in #764" into "those names are never reclaimed" — an open work item restated as permanent design. Both reviewers independently flagged that one; it's the sharpest version of the risk in this whole change, and it's now the "not landed" phrasing the rest of that file uses.

Also fixed: `cargo fmt --all` never sees `tools/hw-gates` — it's a standalone workspace — so my edit there left formatting debris CI could not have caught.

The remaining prose fixes are running. I'll re-verify and push once they land.

content.text:
Done. **Draft PR #1067** — https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1067

## What landed

**449 tracking-issue references gone across 131 files.** 112 of the 123 issues they named were already closed — 91%, matching the issue's own measurement. The sweep is line-neutral by construction: every ref was replaced by the condition it stood for, not deleted along with its sentence.

**The guard** — `scripts/check-tracker-refs.mjs`, a merge-blocking `Tracker Refs` CI job, the rule documented in `AGENTS.md` beside the two comment smells it belongs with, and the gate registered in `blueprint/testing.md` per testing law 1.

## The findings worth your attention

**Six comments were asserting things the code had already contradicted.** `transport.ts` called a shipped broadcast transport "the next slice". `drain.rs` excluded content bytes from a module that owns a full content plane. `op.rs` attributed a quote to `CONTEXT.md` that was actually an issue's scope statement. `grants/create.rs` claimed production impls for a resolver *and* publisher when only the publisher has one. Plus a test doc claiming to be "the write path's first live coverage", and a tooltip shipping `coming soon - #643` to end users.

**The guard's first version was too narrow, and the proof was in `ci.yml` itself.** The security pass found the extension and root lists missed `.toml`/`.json`/`.yml` comments and the `.github` and `scripts` trees — hiding seven live refs, four of them in the very workflow file this PR edits. It also passed vacuously when a root matched no files (reproduced: zero files scanned, exit 0), broke silently at five-digit issue numbers, and let `PR#820` through the qualified-citation exemption. All fixed; 506 files scanned became 611.

**I broke my own new rule in the same diff.** The comment I put on the CI step explained why a `pnpm install` that isn't there isn't there — the absence-justifying shape I added the bullet banning. Deleted.

## Two things I did not do

**`Tracker Refs` is not in `main`'s branch-protection required contexts** — I checked the live list. So the two docs this PR edits currently overstate it: a red gate would merge. That's a repo settings change outside the diff, and it has to happen *after* this merges, or every open PR hangs on a check that never reports. I'd want your say-so before touching branch protection.

**Two-digit `#NN Dn` wayfinder citations stay.** They name decisions in the frozen cipher-box-next corpus, not tickets. One sweep agent stripped two anyway, degrading `(blueprint/engine.md, #33 D6)` to `(blueprint/engine.md D6)` — which attributes the decision to the wrong document. Restored, and I audited the whole diff to confirm no others moved. Worth knowing the security reviewer disagrees with keeping them: a bare `#33` is genuinely ambiguous with cipher-box's own issue #33. Qualifying all ~159 of them is a real follow-up if you want it.

All 26 CI checks passed on the first commit; the review-fix commit is building now. Verification is green locally: 1404 Rust tests, 656 TS, both fmt gates, clippy, wasm32, typecheck, lint. I've left it draft — flipping it ready is what triggers all three reviewers at once, and that's your call.

════════ #1025 ════════
TITLE: engine: rebuild the sweep as an interior-node lazy wave over the real seams
UPDATED: 2026-08-05T08:36:53Z

## Why this is not wiring

`SweepResolver` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`) is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production implementation. #1014 landed the other two — `ChildIndexResolver` and `ScopeRootPublisher` — as `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs::OwnerRotationNet`, and deliberately stopped short of this one because it was blocked on a design question rather than on plumbing.

That question is now answered by **[ADR 0003 — Sweep population, and the below-floor descendant scope root](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0003-sweep-population-and-below-floor-scope-roots.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting.** The answer is not the one the original scope assumed: the resolver could not obtain its work-list because the sweep is walking the wrong population, and the below-floor records it was meant to repair should not be repaired at all.

## What the ADR settles

**The sweep's population is interior nodes, not descendant scope roots.** #26 D2 puts the eager set — the rotated scope root plus every transitively-reachable descendant scope root — under the *cascade*, and gives the sweep the interior nodes that "ride a background sweep re-sealing epoch-lagged nodes". `CONTEXT.md` agrees: epoch lag is "a node whose envelope epoch is behind **its scope's** current epoch". The blueprint's `### sweep` section kept #26 D8's "the work-list is the epoch-lag predicate" and dropped D2's statement of *what* lags, and the implementation followed the blueprint.

**A scope root cannot lag its own floor.** `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both publish first and raise the floor second; `floor::advance_on_unseal` sets the floor equal to the adopted epoch; `minReadEpoch` bumps only on owner read rotations that publish first. So `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root always means the record fetched is not the current one — most often because the parent's `directChildScopeIndex` names it at a name a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved. The gate's stage-5 rejection is correct, and the repair is a pointer consult, not a re-seal.

**Consequently the current `sweep_pass` duplicates the cascade with a vacuous predicate.** It enumerates the eager set and calls `reseal_scope_root` — the cascade's job, landed over the real seams in #1053. Nothing it does can fire in production.

## Scope

1. **Re-target the sweep at interior nodes.** Enumerate the nodes *within* a scope from the scope root's read body, stopping at scope-root boundaries (those belong to the cascade), and select those whose envelope epoch is behind the scope's current epoch. Re-seal each under the current node seed at the current epoch via `net::author::author_child_envelope`, and CAS-publish. This replaces the `reseal_scope_root` path in `sweep_pass`, and `SweepTarget` collapses accordingly — an interior node carries no commitment, ledger, grant blobs, or ascent link, so most of the current struct is scope-root material that belongs to the cascade.
2. **Land the concrete resolver over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`,** reusing `OwnerRotationNet`'s gated read rather than growing a parallel one. With the population corrected it composes with `gated_root`/the child read path unchanged, because its work-list is drawn from records the adoption gate *accepts*.
3. **Route a below-floor scope root through a pointer consult.** Return a distinct *superseded* verdict — neither `Rejected` (a trust violation) nor `Unavailable` (a transport stall) — and have the handler consult that scope's pointer per #38 D4, re-resolve at the re-pointed `currentRootName`, and fail closed only if the fresh record is still below the floor.
4. **Decouple the index self-heal.** #38 D6's repair is "a scope root encountered but missing from its parent's index is repaired and flagged" — detectable from the enumeration walk alone. Run it on the walk result, independent of any epoch comparison. What is implemented today is canonicalisation performed *during* a lag re-seal, which is both a different repair and unreachable whenever the predicate is vacuous.
5. **Fix the grant-creation convergence gate.** `create_read_grant` (`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs`) is `sweep_pass`'s only production caller. Its `SubtreeNotConverged` verdict fires only on a lost CAS race, which only happens on a publish, which only happens for a lagging node — so with a vacuous predicate the gate passes unconditionally and "a new grantee cannot regress through an ancestor scope's history" (#26 D2, `CONTEXT.md` "Epoch-converged") is **unenforced today**. Re-targeting the sweep makes the gate able to fire; it needs its own coverage proving it does, including the negative case.

## Definition of done

- [x] `blueprint/engine.md` `### sweep` corrected and `CONTEXT.md` "Lazy wave" tightened — **done in #1066**, so the blueprint is already normative for this work; read it, don't re-derive it
- [ ] ADR 0003 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint and glossary are maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- An interior node behind its scope's epoch is re-sealed to the current epoch and published; a node already at the epoch is a no-op. Re-running the pass changes nothing (idempotence), and concurrent sweepers are safe under CAS.
- The walk stops at scope-root boundaries — a descendant scope root inside the subtree is **not** swept, asserted explicitly, so the cascade/sweep split cannot silently regress.
- A below-floor scope root whose pointer re-points to a fresh record converges after the consult; one whose fresh record is still below the floor is refused fail-closed. Distinct, asserted outcomes.
- A forged below-floor record is refused, and no consult path admits it.
- A scope root encountered but absent from its parent's index is repaired and flagged **with no node re-sealed in the same pass**, proving the self-heal no longer rides the epoch comparison.
- Grant creation over a subtree with a lagging interior node refuses with `SubtreeNotConverged`, and succeeds once that node converges — the gate proven live in both directions.

## Size

Decided 2026-08-05: **kept whole**, and this issue retitled to match. Scope item 1 is the bulk of it — an interior-node lazy wave needs a new intra-scope walk and a child re-seal path (`net::author::author_child_envelope` exists; the enumeration and the rotation-side wrapper do not), and it invalidates most of the current `SweepTarget`. Items 2–5 are comparatively small once item 1 exists, and they are tightly coupled to it: the resolver's shape, the superseded verdict, and the convergence gate all depend on what the re-target leaves behind. Splitting would have meant a sibling issue whose consumer could not be written until it landed.

Expect a large diff in `crates/engine/src/rotation/` — treat it as a hot-file owner and do not run it in parallel with other `rotation/` work.

════════ #1026 ════════
TITLE: engine: implement the concrete WriteWavePublisher over the real seams
UPDATED: 2026-08-05T08:13:14Z

## Why this is not wiring

`WriteWavePublisher` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`) is the write-plane rotation's transport edge. #1014 landed the two read-plane seams over the real network plane and deliberately stopped short of this one: three of its five methods are plumbing, but `republish` cannot be implemented against the seam as it stands.

Both blocking questions are now answered by **[ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0004-read-body-child-names-on-the-name-wave.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting** — it settles a second, larger gap that this issue originally did not name.

## What the ADR settles

**D1 — the publisher re-resolves; it is not handed the authoring material.** The record handed to `republish` carries only routing identity:

```rust
pub struct RepublishedNode {
    pub node_id: [u8; 16],
    pub new_name: IpnsName,
    pub write_epoch: u64,
    pub is_root: bool,
}
```

Authoring at `new_name` additionally needs the node's read body, the read key it seals under, and the predecessor name. Widening this struct does not work as stated, because the orchestrator does not hold that material either — `WriteScopeNode` is `{node_id, current_name, child_node_ids}` — so it would mean widening `WriteSubtreeResolver` too, and dragging O(subtree) bodies and per-node key material through a primitive that currently holds exactly one secret.

Instead: add **`current_name: IpnsName`** to `RepublishedNode`, and let the concrete publisher do the gated read at `current_name` and author at `new_name`. This mirrors the landed read-plane precedent — `OwnerRotationNet::publish_scope_root` already does exactly this, and says so in code: *"The read body and the envelope fields a republish preserves come from the node's own current record, gated — the rotation carries neither."* The resume contract stays trivially intact: `is_republished(new_name)` is unchanged and still answers from published state alone.

**D2 — the read body cannot be carried verbatim.** `ChildRef.ipns_name` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs`) lives in the **read** body. The wave moves every node in the subtree to a freshly derived name, so afterwards every parent's child refs name nodes that have moved, and once interior old names batch-retire they name nothing.

Write-grantees are fine — they derive names from `writeScopeSeed`. **Read-only survivors cannot**: `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant, and the re-point object carries `currentRootName` and no other name. So without a rewrite, a read-only grantee reaches the new root and cannot descend. #26 D3's "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors" was pointing at exactly this and was never elaborated; the blueprint dropped the clause entirely.

So the wave **rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName`** to the child's freshly derived name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read epoch. Child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known before its parent publishes.

## Scope

1. **Widen `RepublishedNode` with `current_name`** and update `rotate_scope_write`'s call site plus the simulation tests.
2. **Land the concrete `WriteWavePublisher`** over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`:
   - `register` / `retire` over `net::register` and `net::retire` — already bounded and idempotent, reuse rather than duplicate;
   - `is_republished` over the fan-out GET;

## What happened FSM1/cipher-box#1006 asked for a stream-ceiling refusal to read as *recoverable* rather than as a generic failure. It was closed by PR #1065 (`4820773ad`), but **that PR touched zero `apps/web` files** — it delivered the engine and `packages/client` halves only. The web consumer was never written, so the behaviour #1006 describes does not exist for a user. This is not a regression. It is a residual: the plumbing landed and its only consumer did not. ## Verified state on `main` (`bab8d7826`) The engine classifies the refusal and the client carries the classification all the way to the UI boundary: - `crates/engine/src/facade.rs:1335-1363` — `StreamSlot::acquire` enforces `MAX_OPEN_STREAMS` and refuses with a distinct, recoverable error rather than a generic one. - `apps/web/src/engine/snapshotStore.ts:12-16` — `code?: string` on the failure type, documented verbatim as *"carrying the engine's stable code so the UI can classify it."* - `apps/web/src/engine/snapshotStore.ts:154` — `EngineRequestError` is unwrapped into `{ message, code }`. And then nothing reads it: - `rg '\.code\b' apps/web/src` returns **no hits**. No component in `apps/web` branches on the code. - `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/FileBrowser.tsx:15-17` renders every failure identically — a flat `

{error.message}

`. - `FileBrowser.tsx:10` gates the listing on `const settled = !isLoading && error === null`, so **any** error hides the file list (`:26`, `:34`). A recoverable refusal blanks the vault browser exactly as a fatal one does. The net effect: a user who opens one file too many sees their entire file listing disappear, replaced by a raw error string with no indication that retrying will work. ## Scope 1. **Classify on `code`, not on presence of an error.** Split the failure surface into recoverable and fatal. `FileBrowser.tsx` should branch on the code that `snapshotStore` already provides — the field exists and is documented for this purpose. 2. **Keep the last-known-good listing on a recoverable failure.** Decouple `settled` from `error === null` so a recoverable refusal renders as a notice *over* the existing rows rather than instead of them. A fatal error may keep the current blanking behaviour. 3. **Make the notice actionable.** A recoverable refusal is retryable by construction — the ceiling clears when a stream closes — so it needs a retry affordance, not just a message. 4. **Do not invent a code vocabulary in the web layer.** The codes are the engine's; consume the stable strings the facade already emits and fail closed (treat as fatal) on an unrecognised one, so a new engine code cannot silently render as recoverable. ## Gate - A stream-ceiling refusal renders as a recoverable notice **with the file rows still on screen** — asserted on the rows, not only on the notice, so a blanked listing cannot pass. - A fatal failure still blanks the listing and renders as an error. The two paths are distinct and separately asserted. - An unrecognised code is treated as fatal, proving the classification is closed rather than open. - Retrying from the recoverable notice re-drives the pull. ## Notes - **#1064 is affected.** Its premise sentence asserts that "the vault browser renders a recoverable error as a retryable notice over the last-known-good listing" — that is a description of the state this issue *creates*, not of `main`. Read #1064's scope with that correction in mind; the two are adjacent but distinct (this one is the vault browser, #1064 is the media player, which has no component yet). - `apps/web` has no e2e suite on `main` — `tests/` does not exist and `.github/workflows/web-e2e.yml` declares itself dormant. The assertions above land as unit tests now, and should be re-asserted at the e2e tier when #809 rebuilds the harness.
